summary: We developed ASTRAFORGE, a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) space mission lab that runs in any web browser without installation. Users pick a destination from low Earth orbit to Neptune, choose a launch date on a porkchop plot computed from JPL ephemerides, design a spacecraft with real engines, launchers, solar panels and RTGs, and launch it. Real orbital mechanics and live NASA data, such as DONKI space weather, decide whether the mission succeeds, and every failure explains why and how to fix it. Because space should not be only for those with big budgets, ASTRAFORGE also offers five hands-on routes starting at USD 0, from a water rocket to an educational CubeSat, with materials lists, physics calculators, safety rules and a world map built on NASA POWER climate data that shows where and when to launch. It also explains how real NASA missions are built and priced. This matters because professional mission-design tools are complex and built for experts, while most educational resources are animations without physics. ASTRAFORGE turns NASA's open data into active, hands-on learning for any student, anywhere.
details:
What it does. ASTRAFORGE has four sections:

  1. Mission simulator. Users pick one of 9 destinations, from low Earth orbit to Neptune. They select a launch date on a porkchop plot of 2,080 Lambert trajectories per destination, then design the spacecraft: payload, instruments, chemical or electric propulsion, an optional upper stage, solar panels or RTGs, and the launcher. Every console then votes GO / NO-GO. The flight is animated in a 3D Solar System and a first-person cockpit, and it ends with a downloadable mission report.
  2. Learn & Launch (from USD 0). Five real routes: water rocket, model rocket, CanSat, stratospheric balloon and educational CubeSat. Each one has a bill of materials with free alternatives, a physics calculator, step-by-step instructions, safety rules and permits, and a timeline of what happens after launch. A world map scores launch viability from 0 to 100 for the chosen route and date using NASA POWER climatology for wind, rain, cloud cover and temperature. It covers 35 cities, 16 spaceports and a 407-point global grid.
  3. Processes and costs. It walks through the seven phases of the NASA project life cycle (NPR 7120.5, Pre-A to F) with their reviews and decision points, plus launch day in ten steps. A parametric price model estimates a mission's full cost, either for a mission class or for the mission designed in the simulator, and compares it with 16 real missions.
  4. Free mode. A budget slider from USD 0 to over USD 300 billion shows what is achievable at 11 levels, with real examples. A builder combines 7 parts, from free to agency level, and a design review flags impossible combinations.

How it works. Everything runs in the browser.

Orbital mechanics:

  • Planet positions come from JPL Keplerian elements (Standish).
  • Transfers are solved with a universal-variable Lambert solver and patched conics.

Mission engineering:

  • The Δv budget is evaluated phase by phase with the Tsiolkovsky equation.
  • It includes finite-burn gravity losses (Robbins), cryogenic boil-off and low-thrust Δv (Edelbaum).
  • Solar power falls off as 1/d², and RTG output decays over time.
  • Crew radiation dose is based on MSL/RAD measurements and checked against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.

Real-world inputs:

  • NASA DONKI sets a space weather index that can put the launch on HOLD and adds a solar particle event dose reserve.
  • The low-budget calculators use an adiabatic water rocket model, certified A8-3, B6-4 and C6-5 motors, the Cambridge (CUSF) balloon burst method and CanSat parachute descent.

The model is validated against real missions. For example, it gives 543 m/s for Juno's orbit insertion (actual: 542 m/s) and 27,570 km/h for ISS orbital speed (actual: 27,580 km/h).

Benefits. Professional mission-design tools are complex and built for experts, and most educational resources are animations without physics. ASTRAFORGE turns orbital mechanics into active learning:

  • Free and accessible: no installation, works offline with labeled reference data, and is available in English and Spanish.
  • Transparent: every number shows its equation and source.
  • For the classroom: guided challenges and designs that can be shared by link.
  • For any budget: it addresses students and communities with no money at all, so they can start building real projects today and follow a path toward a CubeSat in orbit.

Goals. We want any student, teacher or astronomy club, anywhere, to experience how real missions are planned, built and priced, and to take a first practical step into space engineering regardless of budget.

Tools. React 18, TypeScript, three.js (3D), Tailwind CSS, Vite and lucide-react. The code is modular: data, physics, 3D, UI and features live in separate folders, and all translations sit in a single dictionary. It was tested with Playwright, and the demo video was rendered frame by frame with Playwright and FFmpeg.
